generation.hypothesis: The ultrafine-grain microstructure obtained via stationary friction processing can improve the oxidation resistance of AlCoCrFeNi high entropy alloy.
generation.conditions: Isothermal oxidation in laboratory air at 850, 950, and 1050 °C for 100 h
generation.structural_mediator: Ultrafine-grain microstructure and high grain boundary density
generation.mechanism: The enhanced oxidation resistance is attributed to the ultrafine-grain microstructure and high grain boundary density, which facilitate rapid outward diffusion of Cr ions to form a dense, protective Cr₂O₃ layer, followed by the formation of Al-rich inner oxides via inward oxygen diffusion; the high surface free energy also suppresses the formation of nonprotective spinel oxides.
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved oxidation resistance with reduced oxidation kinetics and cumulative mass gain
generation.baseline: As-cast AlCoCrFeNi high entropy alloy without stationary friction processing
generation.boundary: The oxidation resistance improvement is limited to the specific temperature range and alloy composition
generation.uncertainty: The exact mechanism of oxidation resistance improvement may vary depending on the specific processing conditions and alloy composition

falsification_experiment.design: Compare the oxidation resistance of as-cast and stationary friction processed AlCoCrFeNi high entropy alloy at different temperatures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the oxidation resistance of the as-cast alloy is similar to or better than the stationary friction processed alloy, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: Paper card. Question: How does an ultrafine-grain microstructure, obtained via stationary friction processing, affect the oxidation behavior of AlCoCrFeNi high entropy alloy?. System: Equimolar AlCoCrFeNi high entropy alloy (HEA). Processing: Stationary friction processing (SFP) using a WC-cylindrical tool (12 mm diameter) at rotational speeds of 400 rpm and 1800 rpm for 5 min duration. Test conditions: Isothermal oxidation in laboratory air at 850, 950, and 1050 °C for 100 h. Findings: Grain size refined from 98 μm (as-cast) to 1 μm (SFP_400) and 0.43 μm (SFP_1800).; Phase transformation from BCC/B2 to FCC occurred, with 38% and 55% FCC fraction for SFP_400 and SFP_1800, respectively.; Surface free energy increased by 29.8% for SFP_400 and 35.2% for SFP_1800 compared to as-cast.; Oxidation kinetics decelerated by 12–20% for SFP_400 and 38–48% for SFP_1800 compared to as-cast.; Cumulative mass gain at 850 °C after 100 h was 0.33 mg/cm² (as-cast), 0.27 mg/cm² (SFP_400), and 0.17 mg/cm² (SFP_1800).; Parabolic rate constants (k_p) at 1050 °C were 23.2 × 10⁻¹³ g²·cm⁻⁴·s⁻¹ (as-cast), 18.4 × 10⁻¹³ (SFP_400), and 8.16 × 10⁻¹³ (SFP_1800).; Processed samples formed predominantly protective
